questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a discussion rule redistributes
questions.learningObjective: identify which power a discussion rule moves between participants
questions.stem: A seminar adopts a rule that only the facilitator may interrupt a speaker who is still speaking. What is that rule's main effect on power inside the group?

options.text: It makes the floor a resource the facilitator controls, so the ability to stop a turn moves from whoever wants it to whoever holds the role
It removes interruption from the room altogether, because a member with a question must now save it for a scheduled slot rather than raise it at once
options.misconception: supplies a consequence the rule does not produce, since the rule changes who may interrupt and not whether interruption is possible

options.text: It equalises speaking time among members, because a single authorised interrupter ends any one member's turn sooner than it would end another's
options.misconception: reports an egalitarian effect, while a rule that concentrates the power to cut a turn short distributes it less evenly

options.text: It hands the floor to whoever currently holds it, because the point of the rule is to protect a speaker's turn from being cut off by anyone else at all
options.misconception: describes protection of the speaker without noticing that the protection is administered, and so assigned, to one role

questions.explanation: A discussion rule is a claim about who may do what to whom, so the useful question is always which member's capacity has grown. Here the capacity to end a turn that was previously distributed across the room, and held by whoever was most confident in using it, is gathered into one office. That is the redistribution. The second option describes a total prohibition, which is a different rule: it removes the practice rather than licensing it. The third claims the rule equalises talk, but concentrating a power cannot be what equalises a room, and a single authorised interrupter in fact decides whose turn is cut. The fourth catches the protective half of the rule and misses the part that matters, which is that protection is now administered by a particular member and can be applied unevenly.
questions.hint: Ask which member can now do something that, before the rule, any member could do.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a speaking-time rule produces
questions.learningObjective: predict the participation pattern a fixed time cap will produce
questions.stem: A seminar caps every turn at two minutes and requires the chair to cut off at the cap. What participation pattern should the group expect this rule to produce?

options.text: Discussion concentrates in the members who can compose a complete point quickly, because the cap rewards speed of formulation rather than time spent thinking
Discussion spreads evenly across the members, because a fixed cap removes whatever advantage one member had over another in getting a first word in
options.misconception: assumes a uniform cap is a uniform distribution of airtime, which is exactly the pattern a cap on length does not by itself produce

options.text: Discussion moves into written preparation, because a member who cannot speak in two minutes can still put the same view in front of the group on paper
options.misconception: describes a second-order consequence of a cap, and ignores the first-order effect the cap has on who fills the airtime

options.text: Discussion becomes quicker to start and quicker to finish, because the cap removes the need for the group to agree how long any particular turn should last
options.misconception: reports a procedural gain, while a cap sets one length by fiat and does not remove the need to decide which claims deserve a second turn

questions.explanation: A time cap is a filter, and the question is what it filters for. Two minutes is enough to state a claim that was already formed, and not enough to reach a claim that needs exploring, so the rule selects for members whose thinking is finished before the floor reaches them. The other options each describe something a cap might seem to do. It does not spread the floor: capping the long turns still leaves the number of turns open, and the members who begin from a finished view will take and use them. It does not shift the work to writing, because nothing in the rule requires anyone to write anything down. And it does not settle the group's problems about time, since the cap answers how long a turn may be while leaving untouched whether one turn deserves to become two.
questions.hint: Ask which members can afford to use the full two minutes without having decided in advance what they will say.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Argument against a rule against interruption
questions.learningObjective: answer the argument that a discussion norm protects fluency rather than argument
questions.stem: A member proposes abolishing the seminar's rule against interruption, arguing that the rule protects eloquence rather than argument. Which reply answers that argument most directly?

options.text: The rule can be applied to an evasion as well as to a contribution, so what the rule protects is the reason offered and not the manner of offering it
The rule is a matter the department settled, so a member who prefers a different one should raise it through the channel that exists for such changes
options.misconception: redirects a substantive argument into procedure, which leaves the member's charge about the rule's effect unanswered

options.text: Fluency is not an advantage anyone gains from in a seminar, so a rule that favours it turns out to protect nothing that matters to the members it governs
options.misconception: denies the premise outright instead of showing that the rule's content is the reason rather than the delivery

options.text: Interruption is how a group discovers that it has misunderstood, so a rule forbidding it removes a check the group needs on its own comprehension
options.misconception: argues for limited interruption, and so partly grants the member's case rather than answering the charge made

questions.explanation: The member's charge has a shape: if the rule protected eloquence, then the rule is bad, because eloquence is not the seminar's business. The reply that wins is the one that takes the rule's content away from the member: a rule against interruption can be enforced against a speaker who breaks off to change the subject, which is a failure of reason and not a triumph of delivery. The fourth option is a serious argument and is often the best one in the room, but it is an argument for building an exception into the rule, which concedes rather than refutes. The second treats the question as one of channels, and the third denies the premise by assertion. Only the first shows that the rule's operation does not track fluency at all.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule is actually enforced against, and whether that is a matter of how a claim was expressed.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Argument against a rule against personal remarks
questions.learningObjective: defend a norm against personal remarks against the claim that remarks about a person are remarks about an argument
questions.stem: A member says the seminar's rule against personal remarks is pointless, since remarks about a person are remarks about a person's argument. Which response answers the member's claim?

options.text: A claim about someone's motive is not testable against any record the group keeps, while a claim about what they argued can be read back from the minutes
Personal remarks are ordinary in professional life, so a seminar that forbids them trains members in a register they will meet hardly anywhere else
options.misconception: makes the norm's realism the issue, and leaves the member's claim about what personal remarks are about untouched

options.text: The rule cannot be enforced without a committee, and a group that cannot police personal remarks has no standing to write one
options.misconception: objects to enforceability, which is a different objection from the one the member made about the rule's content

options.text: Personal remarks often carry real information about how a speaker understands their own claim, so banning them removes a source the group would otherwise have
options.misconception: grants the member's point that a remark about a person can bear on an argument, and does not contest it

questions.explanation: The member's claim collapses two things: a claim about the content of someone's argument, and a claim about the person making it. A group can test the first against its own record, because the record shows what was argued. A claim that someone argued a position because of who they are, or in order to be a certain sort of person, has nothing in the record to be compared with, and every member of the room is left as the only possible evidence. That asymmetry is what the norm is for, and it is why the rule is a rule about checkability rather than a rule about politeness. The fourth option is the member's own claim stated in plainer words, and a response that agrees with the premise is not a response to it.
questions.hint: Ask what the group could check against its minutes if a remark is about a person's motives.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a rule against ad hominem costs
questions.learningObjective: identify the resource a norm against personal criticism removes
questions.stem: A seminar bans criticism that addresses the person rather than the claim, and a member observes that personal criticism has since become much harder to argue for in the room. What has the group given up?

options.text: A route for raising the possibility that a position is held for personal reasons, which the norm makes hard to state without also breaching it
Any ability to assess a speaker's sincerity, since a group that may not discuss character has no way at all of forming a view about it
options.misconception: inflates the norm's effect into a general ban on forming impressions, when the norm restricts what a member may argue

options.text: A freedom some members valued, since a group that bans personal criticism is withdrawing a licence it had previously granted the room
options.misconception: describes the norm as a withdrawal of permission, whereas personal criticism was never a permission anyone was granted

options.text: The speed with which the group settles disputes, since criticism of the person was what allowed a contested claim to be closed quickly
options.misconception: credits personal criticism with a speed the norm never affected, and says nothing about what the norm actually removed

questions.explanation: Every norm has a cost, and the honest way to state this one's cost is to name the move it blocks. There is a real question in a seminar: is this position held because it is the position, or because of what holding it does for the person holding it? That question can be asked, and the norm makes it nearly impossible to ask, because the phrasing that puts the question on the table is usually the phrasing the norm prohibits. The trade is therefore not between politeness and candour in general. It is between a rule that keeps almost all of the group's attention on claims, and one narrow but real line of enquiry about the relation between claims and their holders.
questions.hint: Ask what question about a speaker a group can no longer easily raise once the norm is in force.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The standard set by intellectual honesty
questions.learningObjective: state what standard a norm of intellectual honesty sets
questions.stem: A seminar norm says members must represent their evidence as it actually stands, including the parts that count against them. What standard does that sentence set?

options.text: A standard about the fit between a member's confidence and the strength of what backs it, not a standard about reaching any particular conclusion
A standard of correct belief, on which a member who ends up holding the wrong view has failed the norm however carefully they reported the evidence
options.misconception: makes honesty a condition of arriving at the right answer, which converts a norm about reporting into a norm about outcomes

options.text: A standard of candour about private intentions, on which honest reporting of evidence cannot be separated from honest reporting of why the evidence was chosen
options.misconception: extends the norm into the area of motive, which the sentence about evidence does not reach

options.text: A standard of shared doubt, on which any claim no member fully believes is set aside until the group has gathered more evidence
options.misconception: turns a norm about accurate reporting into a norm about suspending judgement, which is a different rule

questions.explanation: Intellectual honesty is often described as a commitment to truth, and the description is what produces the second option. But the norm as written is about a relationship between a member and their evidence: the confidence the member signals should be the confidence the evidence supports, and the report should include what weakens the case. Nothing in that requires the member to end up anywhere in particular, and a member can satisfy it exactly while holding a position the group later abandons. The fourth option confuses honest reporting with a rule about collective decisions, and the third reaches past what the sentence says into a question about why a member chose the evidence in the first place.
questions.hint: Ask whether the norm constrains the conclusion a member reaches or the way a member reports what supports it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Risk of a norm of charitable interpretation
questions.learningObjective: identify how a norm of charity can be used against the speaker it protects
questions.stem: A seminar norm asks members to put an opponent's argument in its strongest available form before criticising it. Which failure does the norm make possible?

options.text: The argument is repaired in the criticiser's hands and then criticised in the repaired form, so the objection lands on a position nobody advanced
A speaker is held to a position stronger than the one given, because a charitable reading is then treated as the view the speaker really held
options.misconception: describes the effect as a burden on the speaker, when the characteristically bad outcome is a criticism with no target in the record

options.text: A weak argument goes unmentioned, because the norm's requirement obliges the group to find a better one before it may say anything at all about the original
options.misconception: makes the norm a gag on criticism, whereas it constrains the version criticised and not whether criticism occurs

options.text: Disagreement is postponed indefinitely, because the search for a stronger version has no point at which the group is permitted to stop searching
options.misconception: turns an effort requirement into a time problem, and misses that the version criticised is the thing that changes

questions.explanation: The norm exists because weak versions of arguments are easy to defeat and defeating them teaches nothing. Its cost is the mirror image: the strong version is constructed by the criticiser, and once constructed it is the only version in the room. If the construction involves supplying a premise the speaker never offered, the criticism that follows is impeccable as reading and useless as argument, because the speaker cannot answer for a position they did not take. This is why charitable reading is a discipline rather than a gesture. The reading must stay inside what the speaker said, and the criticiser has to be able to point at the words the stronger version rests on.
questions.hint: Ask whether the version being criticised can be traced back to something the opponent actually said.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Cost of a bare disagreement
questions.learningObjective: explain what a disagreement without a reason removes from a discussion
questions.stem: A member rejects another member's claim with two words and no reason, and the chair asks what the objection rests on. What does the bare form cost the group?

options.text: It removes any handle for checking the disagreement, because without a stated position nothing in the exchange can be compared with the claim it rejects
It removes the objecting member's standing in the room, because a member who cannot state a reason has no business objecting to anything
options.misconception: makes the cost a matter of status, when the loss falls on the group's ability to test what was said

options.text: It wastes the group's time, because an objection carrying no reason can only be met by asking again for the reason that was withheld
options.misconception: describes the delay to the exchange and leaves the deeper loss, the missing thing to argue with, unstated

options.text: It obliges the objector to argue a position they never held, since a member obliged to reply to a bare objection ends up defending something the objector did not claim
options.misconception: puts the burden on the objector, whereas the person who must supply a position is the one who objected without giving one

questions.explanation: A disagreement is only useful to a group if it puts something in the room that can be examined. When a member says only that a claim is wrong, the group has a verdict and no content: there is no position to weigh against the claim, no implication to show is untenable, and no premise to press on. What remains is a social event, and the chair's request for a reason is the moment at which the exchange can be rescued or lost. This is not a demand that objections be polished. A member may object in a single blunt sentence, provided the sentence names a feature of the claim that the group can argue about.
questions.hint: Ask what a group has in its hands to argue with once a claim has been rejected without reasons.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Difficulty of citing an opponent fairly
questions.learningObjective: explain what makes fair attribution of a position harder than quoting it
questions.stem: A member must set out an opponent's position in a written summary of a seminar's discussions. What makes the fair version the harder part of the job?

options.text: The position has to be restated in words the opponent would accept as their own, which is a further step beyond finding and reproducing the remark itself
The summary cannot be checked, since the opponent is absent and there is nobody present to confirm that the paraphrase does not shift the position
options.misconception: claims the task is unverifiable, while the minutes and the opponent's own later writing are both available as checks

options.text: The summary cannot be corrected afterwards, since a written account of a meeting has to stand once it is written and cannot be amended by those it describes
options.misconception: asserts a fixity the writing does not have, since an author who learns of a distortion can issue a correction

options.text: The summary has to decide which remarks count as the position, since a long discussion contains many remarks and the position is spread across them
options.misconception: identifies a selection problem and stops short of the rewriting, which is where the unfairness actually enters

questions.explanation: Quotation is mechanical and attribution is not. A member can copy a sentence exactly and the record will show whether the sentence was said. Restating the position requires choosing which claims were load-bearing, and a paraphrase that selects the wrong ones will sound entirely fair while reporting a different argument. The test the writer needs is a specific one: could the opponent read the sentence and say yes, that is my view, without wanting to amend it? If the sentence contains hedges or priorities the opponent did not assign, the summary has become the writer's version. This is why a fair summary is longer work than a quotation and why it is the part that gets skimped.
questions.hint: Ask whether the opponent would recognise the restated position as their own without wanting to correct a word.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Confidentiality and a conflicting reporting duty
questions.learningObjective: reason about a norm of confidentiality that meets a reporting obligation
questions.stem: A handbook tells members to keep discussion confidential, and separately requires any member who witnesses misconduct to report it. What follows when a member's witnessed incident meets both duties?

options.text: The member faces two obligations pulling in opposite directions, and neither rule can be applied to the case without first settling what the other one reaches
The later duty simply replaces the earlier one, so once a reporting requirement exists the confidentiality promise stops applying to anything at all
options.misconception: lets the newest rule erase the oldest wholesale, rather than narrowing it in the one place where the two come into contact

options.text: The confidentiality promise binds members to one another only, so it carries no weight against a duty owed to an office outside the seminar
options.misconception: treats a duty owed to outsiders as automatically superior, which the handbook itself does not say

options.text: The member may honour whichever duty is easier, since two rules that conflict in this way are conventionally held to bind with equal force and equal discretion
options.misconception: grants a discretion neither rule contains, and mistakes equal force for a choice between them

questions.explanation: This is a case where the two rules are each defensible on their own terms and the member is caught between them. Neither text mentions the other, so the conflict cannot be dissolved by reading either rule more attentively. It has to be settled by a further judgement about scope: what kind of thing the promise was made about, and whether an incident of this kind falls inside that description. Members in a seminar like this disagree about the right answer, and that disagreement is not a sign the framework is broken. It is the framework asking a question it deliberately did not answer in advance.
questions.hint: Ask what the confidentiality promise was made about, and whether the incident is a thing of that kind.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Scope of consent to record
questions.learningObjective: state what a recording agreement covers and what it leaves open
questions.stem: A chair asks whether anyone objects to recording a seminar session, nobody objects, and the recording begins. What has the group agreed to?

options.text: That one recording of that session, and not what will later be done with the file once it exists
That session and any later use of its recording, because a group that tolerated the making of a record can hardly object to what is done with it afterwards
options.misconception: extends consent to later decisions, which nobody had before them when the question was put

options.text: Any audio record of the seminar made by anyone, since the group's willingness to be recorded does not depend on which member operates the device
options.misconception: generalises one agreement to a category of acts the group was never asked about

options.text: Nothing enforceable, since a room that stayed silent when asked had not agreed to anything and the recording was therefore unconsented from the start
options.misconception: takes the contested view that silence is not agreement, and presents one side of a live question as settled

questions.explanation: Silence after a direct question is treated as agreement in a great many settings, and reasonable people contest whether that treatment is defensible when the question is asked to a group rather than to each person. Whichever side of that contest a reader takes, one thing does not follow: consent obtained for an act is not consent obtained for its consequences. Asking about recording asks about a record being made in a room on a date. Posting, circulating, and publishing are separate decisions taken later by someone, and a group that has not been asked about them has not agreed to them. The scope of what was asked is the whole content of what was given.
questions.hint: Ask what the chair actually asked the group, and whether that question covered anything done with the file afterwards.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Content of a limit on a speaker's identity
questions.learningObjective: distinguish what a norm about identity governs and what it does not
questions.stem: A seminar norm says members should refer to others as those others identify themselves, rather than as the norm's authors would. What is the norm's actual content?

options.text: It governs what members say about another's identity, leaving each member's own view of how to describe someone entirely their own business
It is a statement of manner with no force behind it, since no rule can reach what a member privately thinks about how to describe a colleague
options.misconception: dismisses the norm's effect on speech while granting it none, and so leaves its real content undescribed

options.text: It transfers the question of how to describe a member to whoever mentions the description first, so that member's later usage becomes the group's standard
options.misconception: invents a delegation mechanism, whereas the norm points to the subject's own account and to nobody else

options.text: It covers only descriptions carrying a legal status, since a self-description with no legal standing behind it cannot be what the norm requires of members
options.misconception: imports a legal criterion the norm does not mention and that has no bearing on how people describe themselves

questions.explanation: A norm about identity is easily misread as a norm about what people are permitted to feel, and it is not. What it regulates is speech about other members, and the test it sets is whether the reference the group uses has the subject's assent behind it. What a member privately believes about a colleague's identity is untouched, and a member who privately disagrees has a normal and available move: they can say so, in the room, about the reference, without the norm being invoked against their belief. The limit runs in one direction, and the confusion is common precisely because the norm is described in words about respect, which sounds like an attitude rather than a rule about language.
questions.hint: Ask whether the norm speaks about what members say or about what members are permitted to think.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: How stereotyping operates in discussion
questions.learningObjective: identify how a remark attributes a position to a category
questions.stem: One member asks another, before a discussion of a contested reading, 'You're not going to argue the other side, are you?' and the group moves on. How has the remark worked?

options.text: It treated a position as the property of a category rather than of the member, so the member's freedom to argue it was withdrawn by an inference nobody argued for
It tested the second member's preparation, since a question about which side a person will argue is a reasonable way to find out who has read the chapter
options.misconception: recasts the remark as a preparation check, ignoring that it drew the conclusion rather than testing it

options.text: It raised a doubt about the second member's candour, since a member who hesitates over which side to take is being less than straightforward about what they think
options.misconception: redirects the remark towards sincerity, which the wording does not raise and the group did not act on

options.text: It marked the second member as a less useful participant, which is a judgement about a contribution and so belongs with the discussion of the group's work
options.misconception: reads a value judgement into the exchange, where what the remark did was attach a position to a group of people

questions.explanation: The remark is not an argument, and that is what makes it hard to answer. It draws a conclusion, that this member will not take a particular side, from a fact about the member that has nothing to do with the chapter, and it does so without offering anything for the member to contest. Once the group accepts the framing, the whole range of positions is closed off in advance: the member is not so much argued out of the alternative as never invited into it. Notice also that the remark was a question. A question is a form that invites a reply and, in a room that is being watched, frequently does not get one.
questions.hint: Ask what the remark took to be true about the member before anything was said about the reading.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Representing a viewpoint one does not hold
questions.learningObjective: state the standard governing advocacy of a rejected position
questions.stem: A member agrees to argue a position she has explicitly rejected, on the ground that the group should hear the strongest case for it. How should she proceed?

options.text: Make the case as its holder would, and mark clearly where she is reporting the position rather than endorsing it
Give up the endorsement she has already made, because holding a view and arguing it in the same session is a contradiction a group cannot reasonably expect
options.misconception: requires a member to abandon a settled view, which the assignment does not ask her to do

options.text: Add her own objections as they arise, since the group is best served by hearing both the case and the trouble she finds with it
options.misconception: converts the assignment into two tasks, so that the case for the position is never presented on its own terms

options.text: Present the position without comment, since the reason for the presentation is a matter for her and the group and needs no repeating at each step
options.misconception: leaves the hearers unable to tell advocacy from reporting, which is the confusion the marking matters to avoid

questions.explanation: Advocating a position you do not hold is legitimate and common, and it has one condition: the audience has to be able to tell what you are doing. The presentation must be the one the position's holder would recognise, which means no subtle steering, no ironised emphasis, and no closing move that signals what the presenter privately thinks. Separately, the presenter has to keep her own view marked, because a group that cannot tell whether a summary is reporting or endorsing will draw the wrong conclusion from a summary that happens to be accurate. The fourth option is the tempting one, since restraint feels like respect for the position, and it is exactly the restraint that makes the exchange unusable.
questions.hint: Ask what the hearers would need in order to tell advocacy from agreement.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A norm against false dichotomy
questions.learningObjective: state what a norm against false alternatives is aimed at
questions.stem: A seminar norm forbids setting out two options when more than two are available. What is the norm aimed at?

options.text: The compression of a real range into an apparent pair, which makes agreement between the two look like the only outcome still on the table
Questions that carry three or more parts, since a question of that shape cannot be answered with a yes or a no from the floor
options.misconception: makes the number of parts in a question the target, when what the norm restricts is the set of options offered

options.text: The return of an option the group has already rejected, since an option that has been voted down becomes a false alternative by being named again
options.misconception: treats losing a vote as disqualification, which is not what a norm about offered alternatives says

options.text: The refusal to take a position, since a member who sets out options without choosing among them has declined to contribute a view at all
options.misconception: treats option-mapping as a refusal to argue, when mapping the available options is itself substantive work

questions.explanation: A false alternative works by making the room's map smaller than the territory. If two options are put on the table as exhaustive, then a member who is satisfied with neither must say why neither is acceptable, which is a much higher cost than picking one, and the apparent agreement between the two becomes the path of least resistance. The norm forbids the shrinking, not the choosing: a member may still lay out two options, provided the group also sees the ones that have been left out and why. The third option is the one worth watching in practice, because a rejected option reappearing in a member's summary is a common way the original narrowing gets done a second time without anyone noticing.
questions.hint: Ask what a member must now do if neither of the two options on the table is acceptable.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Checking an imported assumption
questions.learningObjective: describe how a group tests an assumption brought in from outside the text
questions.stem: A member brings a general belief about how a distant group behaves into a discussion of a text, and uses it to explain what the text describes. How should the group test what has been imported?

options.text: Ask the member to separate what the text itself says from the general belief about the practice that the text is being used to support
Ask the member to cite the scholarship establishing the general belief, so the group's challenge takes the form of a check on the member's sources
options.misconception: confuses testing the assumption with checking a citation, and leaves the assumed link to the case untouched

options.text: Substitute a different case from the same region, so the assumption can be tested against a practice the group has not been told anything about
options.misconception: proposes a new case rather than a check, and a counter-case cannot establish what a group would have done

options.text: Put the assumption to a vote, since a general belief the group cannot resolve by argument is the kind of belief a group settles by counting members
options.misconception: settles a question about the world by counting preferences, which is a decision rule and not a test

questions.explanation: An imported assumption enters a discussion looking like background knowledge, and it is hard to challenge because no one in the room said it out loud as a claim. The way to surface it is to insist on the separation: here is what the text establishes about this case, and here is a general belief about such cases that has been brought in from elsewhere. Once the two are apart, each can be dealt with. The text can be read closely, and the general belief can be assessed for accuracy and for how far it reaches. The second option is worth distinguishing, because a group that merely checks the citation of an assumption has done nothing about the assumption's role in the argument.
questions.hint: Ask the member to say, in one sentence, what the text alone would support.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Obligation to inform oneself on a live controversy
questions.learningObjective: state what a member owes when entering a controversy unread
questions.stem: A seminar takes up a live controversy on which members disagree sharply. What does intellectual honesty require of a member who has not read the recent material?

options.text: Saying so, and either making time to read it or marking the parts of their claim that rest on it as provisional until they have
Holding the view they already hold, on the ground that forming an opinion from a summary is a legitimate way of entering a contested question
options.misconception: permits proceeding unmarked, which is what the norm of honest reporting exists to prevent

options.text: Saying nothing until they have read it, on the ground that a member who has not read the material has no standing to speak on the question
options.misconception: converts a disclosure duty into a silence duty, and rules out contribution that can be honestly qualified

options.text: Relying on the reading list, since a reading list is set at the start of term precisely so that members need not do the reading themselves
options.misconception: misreads the purpose of a reading list, which routes the reading to members rather than replacing it

questions.explanation: The obligation is a duty of disclosure, not of silence and not of abstinence. A member who has not read the recent material can take part, and can even hold a firm view, provided the group is told what the view rests on. What honesty rules out is presenting an opinion formed from a summary as though it had survived contact with the material that specialists have read. There is a real cost either way here, which is why the norm is worth stating: marking a claim provisional makes a member's contribution easier to discount, and staying silent keeps a possibly useful perspective out of the room. The norm asks for the smaller of the two costs.
questions.hint: Ask what the group needs to know about a member's basis in order to weigh what the member says.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Standard of evidence for a disputed fact
questions.learningObjective: identify the standard appropriate to a disputed factual claim
questions.stem: Two members dispute whether a reported figure rose or fell across a decade, and neither has the records. What is the appropriate way to settle the fact?

options.text: Produce the records or a source that reports them, since a claim about a figure is settled by what the record shows and not by who is more credible
Let the member who supplied the number keep it, on the ground that attaching a figure to a claim already meets the threshold for making the claim
options.misconception: treats specificity of assertion as a warrant for it, which is the confusion the norm about evidence exists to prevent

options.text: Leave it open, on the ground that a figure from that decade is contested and a seminar has no standing to settle what the records themselves qualify
options.misconception: declines to check a claim that could be checked, treating one group's lack of records as a reason never to look

options.text: Take whichever figure the group's own field uses most often, since a shared convention is the agreed standard for what the number is taken to mean
options.misconception: substitutes a convention for a check, and a convention settles the wording rather than the value

questions.explanation: A disputed fact is a special kind of disagreement, because there is a thing in the world that would settle it, and both disputants would accept that thing if they saw it. That is what makes it different from a dispute about a value, where no such thing exists, and it is why the appropriate response is not a debate about who is more reliable. The test is whether the group can name what would resolve it. If the members cannot, the right conclusion is that the question has not yet been examined, not that it is unanswerable. Members should expect this test to be applied to their own claims, including the ones they regard as obvious.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two disputants would both accept the same piece of evidence if it turned up.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Why a disputed value cannot be proved
questions.learningObjective: explain why the standard for facts does not settle a dispute about values
questions.stem: A seminar argues about which value should govern a course's assessment policy. Why does the standard of evidence used for disputed facts not settle that argument?

options.text: A value is a rule for weighing goods, so the disagreement is about which goods count and no observation of the world can decide between them
A value is a private matter and cannot be falsified, so the only method left for the group is to count how many members hold each position
options.misconception: counts heads in place of reasons, and rests on a contested account of how value claims are related to reasons

options.text: A value claim rests on a factual premise that must be established first, so the argument stalls until the group's factual disagreements are settled
options.misconception: makes the value argument wait on a factual settlement, when the ranking of goods is not the kind of thing a fact can deliver

options.text: A value claim is settled by the consequences it produces, so the group can decide the question by working out which policy works better in practice
options.misconception: substitutes consequences for a ranking of goods, and commits the group to one contestable value argument while thinking it is avoiding one

questions.explanation: Facts and values are settled by different things, and the difference is not that one is knowable and the other is not. A fact is settled by how the world is. A value is settled by which goods the group regards as counting and how they rank, and that ranking is a premise of the argument rather than a conclusion from evidence. So the group can still reason, and it should: it can make its ranking explicit, ask whether the policy it prefers really follows from that ranking, and press the other side to say what its own ranking implies. What it cannot do is wait for a measurement. Whether value disputes admit of rational settlement at all is itself contested, and seminars differ in how they handle it.
questions.hint: Ask what the group would have to observe in the world in order to decide which value governs.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Asymmetry when a member holds an unpopular identity
questions.learningObjective: identify the asymmetry that follows when a claim is discounted for its source
questions.stem: A member's position on a policy is set aside as the kind of thing a person of their background would argue, before its content has been examined. What asymmetry is in play?

options.text: That member has to meet a standard nobody else meets, because their claim is discounted for who is likely to hold it rather than examined for what it says
That member is expected to argue the opposing side as well, on the ground that a view associated with them is subject to a doubled burden of representation
options.misconception: invents a further expectation, where what happened was the removal of a view rather than the addition of a task

options.text: That member's silence will be read as agreement, since a view attributed to them is taken to be theirs whether or not they have ever said it
options.misconception: describes a reading of silence, while the asymmetry in the exchange is that the claim was refused before it was heard

options.text: That member should drop the subject, since a topic associated with their identity cannot sensibly be discussed by the group as a whole
options.misconception: proposes self-exclusion as the remedy, which concedes the framing that produced the problem

questions.explanation: The asymmetry is easy to state and hard to see from inside the exchange. Every other member's claim is assessed on its content, and one member's claim is assessed first on its source, which means the assessment has two stages for one person and one for everybody else. The standard that member must meet is not the standard the group applies to claims; it is a higher one, since the claim must be unusually well made to survive having been doubted in advance. Norms against stereotyping are aimed squarely at this, and they work best when they are stated as requirements about how claims are opened for, rather than as an expectation that members will rise above it.
questions.hint: Ask how many things a member's claim must survive before it is considered on its content.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Options for responding to an offensive text
questions.learningObjective: identify which response to an offensive text leaves something to argue about
questions.stem: A seminar reads a text that some members find offensive, and the group has to decide how to proceed. Which response keeps the discussion answerable to reasons?

options.text: Name the specific feature of the text that is objected to and argue about that, since a general objection to the whole text leaves the group no ground to stand on
Decline to read it, on the ground that a text which offends one member has no place in a seminar that claims to be open to discussion
options.misconception: removes the material instead of meeting the objection, and so settles the session by veto rather than by argument

options.text: Read the whole text and discuss it without comment, on the ground that the group's own discomfort is a reaction to be managed rather than a position to be argued
options.misconception: treats harm as a matter of the group's composure, and gives a harmed member no route into the discussion she was in

options.text: Ask the member to explain her objection privately afterwards, since a public account of the harm would repeat the harm in front of the room it happened in
options.misconception: defers the objection past the discussion, so the group decides about the text before it has heard the only account of the objection

questions.explanation: There is no answer here that is right for everyone, and reasonable members choose differently about texts like this. The question is which option leaves the group something to argue about. A specific objection can be examined: is this the feature that offends, is the objection about the text or about the situation, would the same feature in a different text be equally objectionable. A general objection to the whole text cannot be argued with, because there is no claim in it to accept, contest, or answer, and the group is left with a dispute about whether the session should continue. The remaining options each resolve the situation by removing something, which is a decision a group can take but should take openly rather than by default.
questions.hint: Ask which option puts a claim on the table that the group could accept, contest, or ask about.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A syllabus conflicting with a member's belief
questions.learningObjective: reason about a requirement that conflicts with a member's commitment
questions.stem: A syllabus requires every member to analyse a position the member rejects on religious grounds. What does the course's own stated aim, which is written in analytical terms, require of her?

options.text: That she engage the position as an object of analysis, since examining what a position holds is a different act from endorsing that it should be held
That she withdraw from the course, since an aim she cannot accept in good conscience removes the ground on which the agreement between her and the course rested
options.misconception: treats refusal as the only honest response, and leaves open a reading in which analysis and endorsement come apart

options.text: That the instructor approve an alternative assignment, since a member who cannot meet a stated requirement has to be given a different requirement in its place
options.misconception: supplies a remedy the syllabus does not provide, and so replaces the conflict with a procedural question

options.text: That she analyse the position sympathetically, since an analysis which finds a position wholly wrong is not the analysis the stated aim describes
options.misconception: adds a requirement of sympathy to an aim that asks only for analysis, and constrains her judgement further than the syllabus does

questions.explanation: The distinction the aim relies on is the ordinary one between understanding a position and accepting it, and it does a great deal of work here. A seminar that asks members to analyse arguments they reject is doing something that most people regard as legitimate, and the analysis is not compromised by the analyst's private verdict. What the requirement does ask of her is honesty in the report: an analysis written to make the position look weak is a different document from an analysis that says what the position contains. Members in this situation disagree sharply about what the course owes her, and whether accommodation is owed at all is contested. The answer to the question asked is narrower than that disagreement.
questions.hint: Ask whether the aim requires understanding the position, holding the position, or approving of it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Balanced evidence and what honesty requires
questions.learningObjective: state what a member must report when the evidence is genuinely balanced
questions.stem: The evidence available on a question is genuinely balanced, and each member reads it as favouring their own side. What does intellectual honesty require of them?

options.text: That each member report what the evidence shows without weighting it toward their side, and say plainly where the balance is genuinely close
That each member adopt the view the body of evidence as a whole favours, since a balanced literature is a standing test of whether each member can pick correctly
options.misconception: converts a duty about reporting into a duty about reaching a verdict, which is the substitution the norm is meant to prevent

options.text: That each member state which side the evidence seems to favour, since leaving that unstated conceals the reading that produced the view in the first place
options.misconception: requires a verdict in the other direction, so it commits the same error as the option it is meant to guard against

options.text: That the group record the question as unresolved and move on, since a genuine balance in the literature is itself a finding about the state of the question
options.misconception: makes a declaration of irresolution do the work of a report, and closes off the description of how close the balance actually is

questions.explanation: Honesty in this situation is about the report rather than the verdict. Members will differ in how much weight the balance bears, and some of them will be closer to right than others, but the duty each owes the room is the same: describe the evidence as it stands, including the parts that weaken the case being made, and mark as genuinely close any place where it is. The second option smuggles in a further requirement that nobody can meet, since a member who adopted the view of the whole body might still be closer to the evidence than a colleague who did not. The third is the tempting error, arising from the sense that vagueness is itself a distortion, and it is a distortion in the other direction.
questions.hint: Ask whether the norm governs what a member says about the evidence or what a member concludes from it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Verifying a claim that the group is biased
questions.learningObjective: state what a group must examine before accepting a charge of unfairness
questions.stem: A member tells the group that its discussion last week was unfair to one of its members. What does the group owe the room before it either accepts or refuses the accusation?

options.text: To look at what was actually said to the member concerned, since the accusation is a claim about a record and not only about anybody's intentions
To ask the member concerned what the exchange felt like, since a record of the words cannot show how the exchange was received
options.misconception: confuses a checkable record with an unfalsifiable impression, and lets a feeling stand in for a finding

options.text: To accept the accusation while it is examined, since a member's account of their own treatment carries a weight the group's own recollection does not
options.misconception: pre-judges the question in the member's favour, which decides the outcome before the examination the group was about to make

options.text: To examine the motive of the accusation, since a charge made in anger is more likely to be mistaken about the group's intentions than one made coolly
options.misconception: makes the accuser's state of mind the test, which is a way of dismissing charges without examining what happened

questions.explanation: An accusation of unfairness is partly a factual claim and can be mishandled by treating it as entirely one or entirely the other. The group can look at what was said: how many turns the member got, whether her points were answered, whether anyone spoke over her, and what the minutes record. That will not settle how the exchange felt, and it should not pretend to. But it will settle whether the pattern the member describes actually occurred, and if it did, the group has something to answer for that does not depend on anyone's state of mind. Groups that skip this step tend to end up with either an unexamined accusation on the record or a dismissal nobody finds convincing.
questions.hint: Ask whether the accusation is about something the group could read back from its own record.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A questioned neutrality
questions.learningObjective: answer the argument that a facilitator is not neutral
questions.stem: A member argues that the facilitator ends some members' turns earlier than others and should therefore be replaced. Which response answers this argument most directly?

options.text: The pattern of how turns were ended can be read off the record, so the dispute is settled by examining it rather than by either party's account of fairness
The facilitator exists to apply the rules and cannot also be judged by them, since a person who enforces a rule is not in a position to be examined under it
options.misconception: grants the office an exemption from the standard it exists to apply, which is the claim being challenged

options.text: The appointment was made by the group, so any member may be replaced without needing the facilitator's agreement to the change
options.misconception: answers a question about procedure when the member's charge was about the pattern of interruptions

options.text: Perfect neutrality is unattainable in any discussion, so the demand is unreasonable and the choice of chair is a matter of preference rather than of argument
options.misconception: concedes the premise that a pattern of unequal endings occurred, and moves the question to a ground where nothing can be decided

questions.explanation: The member's charge is testable, and the response that wins says so rather than defending. A chair who ends some turns sooner than others has made a pattern, and a pattern leaves traces: which claims were cut short, how long they had run, whether the claims cut short belonged to particular members. Putting that on the table either shows a consistent practice, which is what the rules call for, or shows an inconsistency, which the group can act on. The fourth option is a concession in disguise, since it agrees that no chair is even-handed and then treats the specific evidence as irrelevant. Neutrality is unattainable; the question the member is actually asking is whether it was aimed at.
questions.hint: Ask whether the pattern the member describes would leave traces anyone could check.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A contradicted claim of inclusivity
questions.learningObjective: state what a group must do about a report its own record contradicts
questions.stem: A group's end-of-term report says its discussions were inclusive. Its transcript shows one member cut off in six consecutive turns. What does the group owe here?

options.text: To correct the report to say what the transcript shows, since a claim about how the term went is a claim about facts and the record is the evidence about it
To keep the report, since one member's experience cannot make every discussion of the term unfair and a single instance is too little to support a general charge
options.misconception: rejects the correction by scale alone, and so accepts a report the evidence contradicts in order to protect its wording

options.text: To keep the report and attach the transcript, so that the disagreement between them is itself an accurate picture of how the term went
options.misconception: turns a defect into a feature, and presents an unresolved contradiction as though it were a finding

options.text: To withdraw the report entirely, since a document shown to be inaccurate cannot afterwards be relied on for anything else it says
options.misconception: infers from one wrong claim that the whole document is worthless, and so discards the parts the record does not contradict

questions.explanation: The claim about inclusivity is not a matter of tone or intention. It is a claim about what happened, made in a document that will be read by people who were not in the room, and the group's own transcript is the evidence about it. Six consecutive interruptions of one member is a pattern, and a report that describes a term without that pattern is inaccurate in a way a reader cannot detect. The group may well conclude that the term was more inclusive than that one sequence suggests, and the report can then say so with the sequence in view. What it cannot do is publish the general claim while knowing about a specific fact that cuts against it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the report is making a claim about a state of affairs or about a disposition of mind.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A speaking-time rule in a recorded session
questions.learningObjective: read a participation pattern produced by a time cap
questions.stem: A seminar caps turns at two minutes and the chair must cut off at the cap. Notes from the third session record nine of eleven turns taken by four members. Each of the seven others spoke once, all in the first ten minutes, for under ninety seconds. The four who spoke most had arrived with the chapter annotated. Which reading of these notes is right?

options.text: The cap converted a difference in preparation speed into a difference in airtime, since members with notes could compose before speaking while the rest had to begin before they had finished thinking
The cap was applied unevenly, since the four members who spoke often were given the whole two minutes while the seven others were cut off before they had finished their point
options.misconception: reports a pattern of truncation, while the notes record the other seven speaking well inside the cap and never cut off

options.text: The seven members used their turn and declined a second, since a cap on length leaves the number of turns entirely in a member's hands and cannot affect how many they take
options.misconception: treats the single turn as a free choice, ignoring that all seven were recorded in the first ten minutes

options.text: The cap produced the participation the rule was written for, since equal turn lengths guarantee that every member gets the same opportunity to speak in the room
options.misconception: confuses equal turn length with equal airtime, which is the outcome the notes show did not happen

questions.explanation: The notes record two things at once, and the reading has to keep both. Members arrived with different preparation, and the cap then let the prepared ones convert that into turns, because two minutes is enough time to open one's mouth and then compose, while it is not enough to reach a view from nothing. The unprepared members spent their single short turn in the opening minutes, which is what happens when a member must speak before the discussion has given her anything to react to. The second option invents an enforcement failure the notes do not report, the third reads a single turn as a free choice when the timing of all seven is recorded, and the fourth mistakes the cap on length for a guarantee of airtime.
questions.hint: Ask what two minutes is long enough to do for a member who has arrived with a note and a page read.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An interruption ruled on in the room
questions.learningObjective: identify what a chair's ruling did to the floor in an exchange
questions.stem: Forty seconds into a two-minute turn, another member says: 'That is not what the passage says.' The speaker stops and does not resume. The chair records the exchange as an interruption and asks the speaker to continue. The speaker replies that the other member has taken the only point she had left to make. What happened in the exchange?

options.text: The chair classified the second member's remark as an interruption, so the floor left a speaker who had not yielded it and the speaker now has to pursue her own turn
The second member put a claim about the passage into the discussion, so the chair rightly ended the first turn and let the disagreement proceed on the text
options.misconception: takes the remark's content as settling the classification, while the exchange turned on who held the floor

options.text: The speaker chose not to resume, and the chair's request simply gave her a second opening that she had not been given earlier in the turn
options.misconception: reads the stopping as a preference, while the speaker's own reply gives a reason tied to losing her remaining point

options.text: The speaker's reply settles the question, since the member who was being spoken over is the best judge of whether her argument had been covered
options.misconception: hands the classification to the affected member alone, and leaves the rule's own terms out of the dispute

questions.explanation: The exchange has a decision in it, and the decision was the chair's. A remark can be about the passage and still be an interruption, and the rule about interruptions is a rule about the floor rather than about content, so the second member's remark did not take the turn simply by being relevant to it. Once the chair recorded the event as an interruption, the speaker was placed in the position of asking for her turn back, and her reply is exactly that: an argument that the interruption was not partial but total. The second option grants the remark its relevance and mistakes relevance for a warrant to interrupt. The fourth is a tempting thought, and it is wrong because the member affected is not the only party with a standing about what the rule requires.
questions.hint: Ask who decided the classification, and what a member's own account settles and does not settle.

questions.topic: A personal remark in answer to a question
questions.learningObjective: identify how a reply about a person differs from a reply about a decision
questions.stem: Asked to explain how the seminar had settled its reading list, a member replies: 'You are only arguing for that now because you did not get your way last time, and everyone in this room knows it.' Which description of the reply is correct?

options.text: It moved from how a decision was reached to why the other member wanted it, and the motive it names is not something anyone in the room can check against a record
It supplied evidence about how the decision was reached, since it identifies the member who had wanted the other outcome and so had reason to press the point now
options.misconception: treats a guess at motive as evidence about a procedure, and mistakes an identification for a cause

options.text: It appealed to what the room already knew, so the claim needed no argument and the burden of denying it lay with the member it named
options.misconception: takes an appeal for shared knowledge as knowledge, and puts the burden of proof on the wrong member

options.text: It was verifiable, since members who were present when the reading list was settled could be asked which way it went and the matter thereby established
options.misconception: proposes a check that would settle a different question, since which list was chosen does not establish why this member argues now

questions.explanation: The reply was asked for an account of a procedure and gave an account of a person instead. That substitution is what the norm against personal remarks exists to catch, because the two do not carry the same evidential weight. A group's minutes can show how a reading list was chosen, and members who were there can testify to what was said. Nothing in the room can settle why a member is arguing now, least of all the member herself, since the reply is about her and she is the person with least reason to accept it. The fourth option is the useful contrast: a check on the outcome exists, and it is the wrong check for this exchange.
questions.hint: Ask what the question asked about, and what the reply answered instead.

questions.topic: An objection that attacks the proposer
questions.learningObjective: identify what an objection about a person's history leaves unanswered

Whether the proposal is new, since the reply shows the member has supported the rule before and the group may treat it as settled practice
options.misconception: converts one member's earlier preference into a decision the group has already made

options.text: Whether the member is consistent, since the reply raises the question directly and consistency is a standard members accept for themselves
options.misconception: credits the reply with raising a testable question, when it makes an assertion and proposes no comparison

options.text: Whether the proposal still fits the group's practice, since the reply places the proposal two years back and a rule from then may not suit the seminar now
options.misconception: reads a reference to the past as a claim about present conditions, which is not what the reply does

questions.topic: A charitable reading that reversed a position
questions.learningObjective: identify an attack on a reconstructed rather than an advanced position
questions.stem: Asked to summarise a colleague's argument, a member wrote that the colleague held that unequal access to a service should not count as evidence about outcomes, since treating it as evidence assumes what it ought to test. At the meeting the colleague had argued the reverse: that unequal access produces unequal outcomes and should therefore count as evidence about them. What did the summary do?

options.text: It reversed the direction of inference before criticising it, so the objection was addressed to a position the colleague never advanced
It added a critical remark of its own, so what the colleague will object to is the summary's judgement rather than the view it attributes to her
options.misconception: treats the critical clause as the main defect, while the attributed view is the reverse of the one the colleague gave

options.text: It kept the colleague's terms, so the disagreement between the two members is about how evidence should count rather than about the position itself
options.misconception: preserves the same position because the same words were used, and overlooks that the inference runs the other way

options.text: It reported the meeting accurately, so the disagreement is about the conclusion the colleague drew from unequal access rather than about what she said about it
options.misconception: treats the summary as faithful and locates the conflict in the conclusion, which the summary's clause also reverses

questions.explanation: The colleague's claim was that unequal access causes unequal outcomes, and that this makes it evidence about those outcomes. The summary reports her as claiming the opposite, and then adds a critical remark that fits the reversed version and not hers. A group reading that summary would conclude that the colleague had argued a familiar, slightly confused position, when in fact she had made a causal argument and the summary has made her into the object of a criticism she never invited. questions.topic: A disagreement with no reason given
questions.learningObjective: identify what a reasonless objection removes from an exchange
questions.stem: A member claims the seminar should weight drafts more heavily in assessment. The response is: 'No.' The chair asks what the objection rests on. The member says the claim is wrong and offers nothing further, and the claim is not raised again that evening. What is the state of the exchange?

options.text: Nothing in it can be tested, because the objection supplied no position for anyone to set against the claim it rejected
The claim was refused by the group, since the chair's request for a reason is the exchange's answer and the claim therefore failed on the evening
options.misconception: reads the chair's question as the group's verdict, when it was an attempt to obtain a reason

options.text: The claim was withdrawn by the member who made it, having found no support once the objection was stated
options.misconception: supplies a withdrawal and a search for support that the record does not mention

options.text: The reason is recoverable from the minutes, so the group can reconstruct what the objector thought even though it was never spoken in the room
options.misconception: invents a record of the reasoning, when the minutes can record only what was said

questions.explanation: The exchange contains a claim and a rejection of it, and no third thing. There is no position stated, no implication offered, no premise pressed on, so the group has nothing it could weigh, agree with, or show to be mistaken. The chair's request is where the exchange could have been rescued, and it is worth noticing that the member's second contribution, saying the claim is wrong, is a repetition rather than an addition. The result is that a claim about assessment weight passed out of the discussion without ever being tested, which is the specific harm a norm about reasoned disagreement addresses and why a rule against reasonless objections is not merely a matter of politeness.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A summary that shifted an opponent's standard
questions.learningObjective: identify how a faithful-sounding summary can misstate a position
questions.stem: A written summary reports an opponent's position as: 'willing to accept a small number of uncorroborated cases when the alternative is a delay in reporting.' Asked to check it, the opponent replies: 'I said I would not treat a case as established without corroboration, which is not a preference for delay, and it is not about how many cases.' What has the summary done?

options.text: It turned the opponent's standard for what counts as established into a statement about timing, so the position reported is not the one the opponent described
It kept the opponent's terms and compressed the remark, so the position is harder to check against the minutes than the sentence it was drawn from
options.misconception: identifies compression as the fault, when the opponent's objection shows the content of the position itself is wrong

options.text: It attributed a willingness the opponent denied, so the question is a dispute between two witnesses and the minutes cannot settle it
options.misconception: treats a checkable attribution as unresolvable, while the opponent's remark fixes what the position was

options.text: It added the group's own disagreement, so a reader would take the preference for delay to be part of the opponent's case rather than the summary's
options.misconception: supposes an editorial opinion that the summary does not contain

questions.explanation: The opponent set a condition on when a case may be called established, and the summary reports a willingness to act without corroboration, traded off against delay. Those are different claims with different implications, and the difference is the sort that changes how a reader would regard the opponent. The summary is not obviously tendentious. It uses the opponent's own words about corroboration, which is why it reads as fair while being wrong, and why checking attribution is harder than checking a quotation. What made the shift visible was the opponent's own restatement, which is the standard a summary has to meet and the reason a group should ask for it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the reported position would make the opponent responsible for anything the original remark rules out.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A report made against a confidentiality promise
questions.learningObjective: identify the interpretive move by which two duties are made compatible
questions.stem: A handbook tells members to keep discussion confidential so that people can say what they think. A member sees a supervisor dismiss a student's question about a marking decision, reports it to a programme office, and when other members call this a breach of the handbook, replies that the handbook is not a promise to protect misconduct. How does that reply handle the conflict?

options.text: It reads the promise as narrower than its authors wrote, so the referral rests on an interpretation of what the promise covered rather than on any stated exception to it
It treats the handbook as creating a conflict, so the referral is a decision about which duty to break rather than a claim about what the handbook meant
options.misconception: keeps the conflict standing, while the reply dissolves it by limiting the promise's scope

options.text: It treats the report as a procedural step, since the handbook's separate requirement to report is what a member who witnessed something is expected to use
options.misconception: invents an expectation the handbook does not state and the member does not appeal to

options.text: It leaves the handbook binding as written, so the other members are right and the member's reading of it is an excuse rather than a finding
options.misconception: settles a question the handbook leaves open, and treats one reading as automatically the correct one

questions.explanation: The reply does not say the reporting duty beats the promise. It says the promise was never about this, which is a move that leaves both rules standing and locates the difficulty in a question of scope. Whether the handbook should be read that way is genuinely contestable, and members often disagree about what a general promise about confidentiality can be taken to cover. What is clear is the shape of the argument, and that is what a group needs in order to discuss it: the dispute is not about which duty wins but about what the promise was a promise to do. A group can work on that question, and it is a better discussion than one about precedence.
questions.hint: Ask whether the member placed one rule above another or changed what the other rule says.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A recording used beyond what was asked
questions.learningObjective: identify what a recording agreement did and did not cover
questions.stem: A chair asks whether anyone objects to recording the session. Nobody speaks, the recording begins, and two weeks later a member finds it posted on a page outside the seminar and asks for it to be taken down. The chair says the group agreed. Which description of the exchange is right?

options.text: The agreement covered making the recording, and the posting was a later decision the chair now treats as having been covered by it
The group agreed to both, since a room that raised no objection to a recording has no ground on which to object to what was done with the file
options.misconception: extends a decision about making a record into consent to a decision about publishing it

options.text: The member who objects cannot rely on the earlier agreement, since the question was put to the room and she did not object at the time
options.misconception: treats silence as waiver of a later objection, which the passage gives no basis for

options.text: The chair's claim is reasonable, since the page is run by the seminar and nobody outside the group was involved in putting the recording there
options.misconception: assumes who runs the page and who placed the file, neither of which the record establishes

questions.explanation: The question put to the room had one content: whether to record this session now. It was answered, in the way the group's practice treats silence. The posting is a separate act, taken by a person some days later, about a destination nobody had mentioned. A consent that covered the later act would have had to be asked for, and the fair way to describe the exchange is that a real agreement was obtained for one thing and then stretched to cover a second. Whether the stretch is defensible is a fair question for the group, and the fourth option is the version of that question written as though the facts had already been established.
questions.hint: Ask what act the question covered, and when the second act was decided by anyone.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A self-description the member supplied nothing for
questions.learningObjective: describe what a group does when a subject declines to supply a label
questions.stem: In a reading group a member is referred to by a label she has not used. Asked what the correct reference is, she says the label is hers to set and declines to give a replacement. The group then uses her initial in all its notes and continues. What has the group done?

options.text: It took the speaker's own account as the thing being consulted, and its practice follows her decision even though she supplied no label to use
It treated the missing label as a gap it had to fill, since a record containing no way to refer to a member is unusable to the readers who come after
options.misconception: describes a necessity the group never invoked, since it chose the speaker's terms over convenience

options.text: It treated the refusal as settling the matter for now, so the practice it adopted is a holding arrangement until a label is supplied
options.misconception: reports the arrangement as provisional, which nothing in the exchange says

options.text: It took the decision out of the speaker's hands, since the group chose an initial she had not proposed and so set a description she had refused to give
options.misconception: treats a group choice as an imposition, while an initial describes no identity and asserts none

questions.explanation: The member set a boundary about description and supplied nothing to fill it, and the group respected the boundary without needing content for it. What the group adopted, an initial, is a way of referring to a record rather than a way of describing a person, and it is the option available that makes no claim about who she is. That is the practical form the norm takes when a member declines to name herself. The fourth option is worth taking seriously and then setting aside, since the danger the norm guards against is a group choosing among labels, and an initial is not one of the labels on offer.
questions.hint: Ask whether the replacement the group used describes the member or merely refers to her.
