questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A position predicted from a field of study
questions.learningObjective: identify how a stereotype closes a position before it is argued
questions.stem: Asked whether he supported the reading of the second chapter, a member says: 'I am sure you will argue the other side, given the field you are from.' A second member replies: 'That is not much of a reason.' The first says he meant it as a joke, and the chapter is not discussed again that session. How has the exchange worked?

options.text: The remark drew a position from a field of study, and the topic being dropped afterwards left the inference standing as though it had settled who would argue what
The remark was withdrawn once a member called it, so the exchange corrected itself and the group needed to do nothing further about it
options.misconception: counts a withdrawal as a correction, and ignores that the topic went with it

options.text: The second member answered with a reason, so the group's standard of reasons was applied and the topic could properly have carried on
options.misconception: counts a restatement of the standard as a satisfaction of it

options.text: The remark asked about the first member's background rather than his view, so it posed a question the group was entitled to put
options.misconception: reads a completed inference as an inquiry, when nothing in the wording leaves the position open

questions.explanation: Two things went wrong and only one of them was addressed. The remark assigned a position to a member on the basis of a field, which is the assignment norms against stereotyping exist to stop. Then the chapter was not discussed, which left the assignment in place without ever being tested, and a reader of the minutes would find the prediction sitting there looking like a fact about the room. Calling it a joke addressed the tone and not the content, and the second member's reply named the defect without removing it. The structural point is that a stereotype in discussion is cheap to utter and expensive to retract, because the group has to spend a whole exchange undoing something said in six words.
questions.hint: Ask what the group would have to do now in order for the position to be genuinely open.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A speaker's request during advocacy
questions.learningObjective: identify the risk a member is managing by asking to be interrupted
questions.stem: A member assigned to present the case against a funding decision says she supports the decision and will argue the case against it anyway. She asks the group to interrupt her if her tone starts to signal approval of the decision. What is she managing?

options.text: Her own delivery, since a case argued by a member who holds the opposite view can carry an endorsement in the voice that the words do not
The group's openness, since she is asking them to keep the decision open for the hour on the understanding that her own view will be set aside
options.misconception: converts a request about her own speech into a request about the group's state of mind

options.text: A likely misunderstanding, since she expects the group to think she is arguing her own position and wants that visible before it takes hold
options.misconception: supposes a misunderstanding the group has not shown, when she names a specific channel for the message

options.text: Her own reluctance, since the request is a way of signalling that she does not want the assignment without withdrawing from it
options.misconception: reads reluctance into a member who has already said she will argue the case

A member arguing a position she rejects can keep every word accurate and still lose the room, because persuasion also runs through emphasis, pacing, and the pause before a concession. Those are the parts a speaker cannot audit while speaking, which is exactly why she asked the group to do it. The fourth option is the one to watch, since reluctance is common and often the honest description of how a member feels about an assigned case. It is not what this member described. She said she would argue it, and she identified a specific risk she wanted the room to watch for her.
questions.hint: Ask what could go wrong in a presentation that the speaker's own words would not show.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A record that narrowed the options
questions.learningObjective: identify how a record presents two arrangements as exhaustive
questions.stem: Minutes record: 'Members agreed that assessment should be either entirely continuous or entirely terminal, and that a mixed system could not be administered fairly.' Three weeks later a member asks what would count as a mixed system, and the chair replies that the alternative is the terminal system already in use. What has the record done?

options.text: It offers two arrangements as the whole field, and the chair's reply then treats one of them as the alternative, so nothing outside the pair has anywhere to go
It rules out a mixed system on administrative grounds, and the chair's reply simply repeats the ground the group gave for ruling it out
options.misconception: reports a stated reason, while the record offers an assertion of unfairness with no reason attached

options.text: It leaves the question open, since finding a mixed system hard to administer is a different matter from ruling one out of order
options.misconception: gives the record credit for a qualification it does not make

options.text: The chair's reply widens the field, since a terminal system and a mixed system are now both named as candidates for the group to consider
options.misconception: reads a narrowed exchange as a broadened one, when the reply is the narrowest statement in the record

questions.explanation: The record does two things. It states a preference between two arrangements, and it asserts that a third kind cannot be administered fairly, which places the whole question of mixed systems outside the field of discussion. The chair's reply confirms the shape, since the alternative to the system in use is now one named option, and the member's question about what a mixed system would even look like goes unanswered because the record has already placed the category out of bounds. A group that wants to catch this should ask of any minute whether the options recorded are the options that were available, or the options that were on the table when the discussion began.
questions.hint: Ask whether the record lists what was available or what was on the table at the time.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A general regularity used to explain a case
questions.learningObjective: identify an argument that explains a case from a pattern rather than a record
questions.stem: A member argues that a text's account of a council's proceedings shows the members were following custom, since a council in that period would not act against custom without outside pressure. Asked to support this, the member offers a general work on councils in the period. A second member has read a different work describing several councils that disregarded custom. What is the structure of the member's argument?

options.text: It explains this council's conduct by appeal to a pattern, so the inference runs from the general case to the particular one and nothing is offered about the particular one
It has been met with a contrary work, so the general belief the member relies on is refuted and the claim about the council cannot stand
options.misconception: overstates a contrary work, since several exceptions show the general claim is contestable rather than false

options.text: It turns on whether outside pressure existed, which is a factual question the group could settle by looking for evidence of it
options.misconception: proposes a check on a premise, and leaves the inference from the premise to this council unexamined

options.text: It is a reasonable opening explanation, since a general regularity is the ordinary starting point for reading a record and does not need case-specific support at that stage
options.misconception: accepts the pattern as a starting point and so allows it to do the work of a finding about this council

questions.explanation: The member's sentence contains two claims, and the second is doing all the work while the first is left resting. What the text records is how a council's proceedings went, and from that the member infers that custom was being followed, and from that infers that a council of the period would not act against custom without outside pressure. The general work supports the last of these, and the last of these is being used to establish the first. A group that presses on the general work has therefore pressed on the wrong end. The counter-work is a useful complication rather than a refutation, and it makes the general claim harder to rely on without touching the inference to the case.
questions.hint: Ask which of the member's claims is evidenced by the text and which by the work.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a rule against interruption secures
questions.learningObjective: identify what a norm must secure before its costs can be weighed
questions.stem: A seminar is debating whether to keep its rule against interruption. First say what the rule secures, then say what it costs. What must the first answer identify?

options.text: That a speaker's turn is at risk of being lost to whoever is quickest to claim the floor, since the costs cannot be weighed until the thing secured is named
That interruptions are a frequent feature of the group's meetings, since a rule is worth debating only where the practice it governs is common
options.misconception: makes prevalence the precondition for a norm, which is a question about how often a thing happens rather than what the rule protects

options.text: That members find interruption rude, since a rule resting on a preference about manner cannot be defended to a member who dislikes it
options.misconception: rests the norm on taste, and so makes its standing depend on agreement about the taste

options.text: That the chair is able to enforce the rule, since a rule nobody can apply is not the kind of thing a group should keep in force
options.misconception: treats enforceability as the first question, while a norm that cannot be enforced is still the group's stated position on a practice

questions.explanation: A cost-benefit argument about a rule is only coherent once the benefit has been named, and the benefit is what the rule is holding in place. Here it is a turn: without protection, the claim a member is part-way through making can be ended by someone who has nothing to add to it. The first answer has to say that, and it has to say it in a form the group can check against its own record, which is why the risk to a turn is better than a claim about members' preferences. The other options each substitute a different question, and all three are questions a group can usefully ask afterwards. They are not the question that makes the later one answerable.
questions.hint: Ask what would be lost, and by whom, if the rule did not exist.

questions.topic: Identifying the part of a reply a norm reaches
questions.learningObjective: identify which sentence in an exchange a norm covers and what it displaces
questions.stem: In a recorded session a member answers another's claim with a remark about that member's motives. First say which part of the exchange the norm about personal remarks reaches, then say what remains to argue. What must the first answer identify?

options.text: The sentence about motives, since the rest of the exchange can only be argued once the offending part has been set aside
The original claim, since that is the statement the norm protects and everything said after it is commentary on the claim
options.misconception: calls the claim the thing protected, while the norm concerns what may be said about a person rather than the claim itself

options.text: The register of the exchange, since a remark made angrily is what a norm about manner among members is aimed at
options.misconception: substitutes tone for content, and the norm restricts what a remark is about rather than how it is delivered

options.text: The order of the two speakers, since the norm binds whoever speaks second and the second member in this exchange is the one who spoke second
options.misconception: attaches the norm to a position in the exchange, while it attaches to the content of remarks

questions.explanation: A norm about personal remarks applies to a part of an exchange and not to the whole of it, and the first job is to locate that part precisely. A remark about why someone holds a position is the part the norm reaches; the claim that was under discussion is not, and the reply's other content, if there was any, is not. Locating the sentence is what makes the second step possible, because a group cannot return to a question it has not established was left unanswered. The second option is the common confusion, and it is worth noticing that it would make the norm almost nothing, since almost every exchange contains a claim somebody would call protected.
questions.hint: Ask which single sentence in the exchange could not have been said about the text.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a case for a rejected position concedes
questions.learningObjective: identify what presenting a position at its best obliges a member to confront
questions.stem: A member is to argue a position she rejects. First say what that case would have to concede in order to be a good case, then say what follows for her own position. What must the first answer contain?

options.text: The premises the case relies on and the costs it conceals, since a case presented at its best is the one the member's own view has to survive
That the position is false, since a member who has stated its premises properly cannot go on holding the opposite view
options.misconception: makes a consistency requirement, when presenting a case and endorsing it are different acts

options.text: That the speaker shares the position, since a case can only be put well by someone who plainly believes it
options.misconception: requires belief as a condition of skill, and would rule out most of the assigned advocacy seminars actually do

options.text: That the group is prepared to accept it, since a case for a position can be put effectively only where the audience is close to persuaded
options.misconception: makes the audience's disposition a precondition, when the point of the assignment is to reach an audience that is not

questions.explanation: Advocacy is an exercise with two outputs, and the second is the harder one. A member who presents a position at its best has made herself responsible for the premises it needs and the costs it hides, and she cannot both present it and step away from that. What follows for her own position is then a real question rather than a formality: she has to say what she accepts from the case, what she disputes, and on what ground. The second and third options both look like standards of good advocacy, and both would make the assignment impossible as specified. The fourth is the wrong way round, since a group that is already persuaded needs no case made to it.

questions.topic: Stating the strongest version of an argument
questions.learningObjective: state what a charitable restatement must satisfy before criticism is addressed to it
questions.stem: A member prepares to criticise an argument made in an earlier session. First state the strongest version of it, then say what follows for the group's own position. What must the first answer do?

options.text: Give the version its holder would accept as their own, since a criticism of anything weaker answers a claim nobody advanced
Give the version most members find persuasive, since the reading a group is drawn to is the one most worth examining
options.misconception: sets the audience's response as the test, and so builds a version the holder may not recognise at all

options.text: Give the shortest version that can be criticised, since a long argument carries more claims than a single reply can address
options.misconception: trims for manageability, which gives a shorter version rather than a stronger one

options.text: Give the version as it would be put with its author present, since an argument is generally clearer once its author can answer for it
options.misconception: supplies an imagined conversation, where the standard is what the record shows was actually claimed

questions.explanation: The test for a charitable restatement is whether the holder would accept it, and the reason is practical rather than charitable. If the version differs from what was said, then a reply addressed to it can be turned aside with a correction, and the group has spent its time on a position nobody held. The second option is a version the group finds persuasive, which is a different project and one the speaker has no obligation to authorise. A factual disagreement about what discussion does, since their accounts of its effects could in principle be compared against each other

options.text: A disagreement about procedure, since the two positions differ in the method each would use to reach a conclusion in the room

options.text: A disagreement about standing, since each member claims a different kind of authority to settle the question for the group
options.misconception: supplies an appeal to authority that the exchange does not raise

Protection and rigour are both defensible goods, and the two members are not disagreeing about any fact that could be checked. They are disagreeing about which of the goods the seminar is for, which is a premise of their positions rather than a result of them. Once that is on the table, the group can reason: ask each member what their preference implies for a hard case, whether they would trade it away, and what they think the seminar is for. questions.topic: Scope of a confidentiality promise

That the promise was made in writing, since an undertaking a member cannot point to afterwards is the kind nobody can be held to
options.misconception: makes the form of the promise the question, while the difficulty is what it covers rather than how it was recorded

options.text: That the promise was made to the group, since a promise made to a single person is a weaker undertaking than one made to everyone
options.misconception: compares two kinds of promise, and the difficulty is not who was the beneficiary

options.text: That the promise admits no exceptions, since a promise with exceptions cannot be applied consistently from one case to the next
options.misconception: decides the question of exceptions in advance, when that is the very question the member has to face

questions.explanation: Two duties that point opposite ways cannot be reconciled by ranking them, because neither is the superior of the other on the face of the rule. What settles the case is a reading of scope: the promise was made about something, and the question is whether what the member witnessed is a thing of that kind. Answer that first and the second step follows, whether it is that the reporting duty applies untouched or that the promise is broken and the member must say so. The fourth option looks rigorous and is a mistake, because a promise whose scope is unclear is exactly the case where a group has to reason rather than apply a formula. questions.topic: What a reasonless objection would need

options.misconception: adds a requirement of citation, which the objection does not need in order to be argued with

options.text: An acknowledgement of discourtesy, since a bare rejection of a colleague's claim is a discourtesy the group should mark before proceeding
options.misconception: converts an evidential gap into a matter of manners

options.text: A vote, since an objection with no stated position can only be settled by the members rather than by argument
options.misconception: substitutes counting for reasoning at the point where the reasoning is missing

questions.topic: What a balanced evidence base obliges
questions.learningObjective: state what members must report when the evidence is evenly balanced
questions.stem: The evidence available in a discussion is genuinely balanced. First say what that obliges each member to do, then say what the group should record. What must the first answer contain?

options.text: That each member report the evidence without weighting it toward their own side, since the duty attaches to the reporting and not to the conclusion
That each member wait for more evidence before taking a view, since a balanced body of work is by definition an incomplete one
options.misconception: makes a balanced literature an unfinished one and so defers the question rather than answering it

options.text: That each member say which side the evidence seems to favour, since leaving that unstated conceals the reading that produced the view
options.misconception: requires a verdict in the name of candour, and so relocates the problem instead of reporting it

options.text: That each member accept that the question may be unanswerable, since a genuine balance is a permanent feature of the literature on it
options.misconception: turns a report about the present evidence into a prediction about the whole field

questions.explanation: Balance is a fact about the evidence, and it is a fact every member is entitled to be told. The obligation is therefore on the reporting, and the second answer then follows: the group's record should say what the evidence contains, including where it is close, so that a reader of the minutes can see that the division in the room was not simply two members shouting past one another. This is a small procedural point with a large effect on how a term is understood afterwards. The third option is the error that the norm most often produces, since vagueness about which side the evidence favours is its own kind of distortion, and a demanded verdict does not fix it.
questions.hint: Ask what a member owes the group about the evidence as opposed to the view built on it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A rule that puts a gate on the floor
questions.learningObjective: identify the power a recognition rule transfers
questions.stem: A group debates replacing its open floor with a rule that a member must be recognised by the chair before speaking. Four descriptions of the change follow. Which one describes what the rule does?

options.text: It puts the chair on the route into the exchange, so who may begin a contribution becomes a matter for the role rather than for the floor
It secures a place in the exchange for every member, so the change is a gain for the members who would otherwise have been passed over
options.misconception: describes an equalising effect, while a rule that inserts a gate delegates admission rather than distributing it

options.text: It narrows the discussion to the members who have prepared, since recognition is the chair's signal that a contribution is worth hearing
options.misconception: reports an effect on the quality of contributions, which is not what the rule is a rule about

options.text: It alters only the order in which members speak, since recognition decides when a member speaks and not whether a member may speak
options.misconception: reduces the rule to sequencing, while a member who is never recognised does not speak at all

questions.explanation: The group's question is what the change transfers, and the answer is admission. Under an open floor, who speaks is settled by members, and the price is that a confident member can hold the room. Under a recognition rule, the chair decides who begins, and the price is that the group's fairness now depends on a single person applying a judgement that nobody else in the room gets to see. A group considering such a rule should weigh that against the problem it was meant to solve, and should consider whether the recognised-not-recognised distinction will itself be made fairly. None of the other descriptions is what the rule does, however useful it would be if it did.
questions.hint: Ask which member gains the power to say no before a turn has begun.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The participation a short cap produces
questions.learningObjective: identify which capacity a speaking-time rule selects for
questions.stem: A group caps every turn at ninety seconds. Four descriptions of the participation that follows follow. Which one does the cap produce?

options.text: It selects for members who can state a finished point quickly, so the rule rewards a kind of fluency rather than a kind of preparation
It leaves the pattern of participation as it was, since a rule about how long a turn may be does not affect who decides to take one
options.misconception: claims the cap has no effect on distribution, which is precisely the question at issue

options.text: It moves the preparation into writing, since a member who cannot speak in ninety seconds can still put a view in front of the group on paper
options.misconception: describes a consequence the rule does not require anyone to take

options.text: It spreads the floor more widely, since a short turn is easier for a quiet member to claim than a long one is
options.misconception: assumes short turns lower the cost of speaking, when they lower the time available to prepare what is said

questions.explanation: Ninety seconds is a budget, and a budget rewards whoever can produce a finished claim within it. The members who benefit are not necessarily the ones who have read most, though they often overlap, since it is the ability to arrive with a view rather than to find one in the room that the cap pays for. A group that wants the cap to change the distribution of preparation has to pair it with something else, such as written preparation circulated in advance, because the cap alone changes who is audible and not what they arrive with. The second and third options assume effects the rule does not produce, and the fourth mistakes a shorter turn for a more accessible one.
questions.hint: Ask what a member can do with ninety seconds, and what a member cannot.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Responding to a text that offends
questions.learningObjective: select the response that keeps an objection arguable
questions.stem: A seminar reads a text that a member finds degrading to a group she belongs to. Four responses follow. Which one keeps the matter arguable?

options.text: She identifies the passage and the particular feature of it she objects to, which gives the group a claim to examine rather than a verdict to absorb
She asks for the text to be replaced, which respects her position and lets the rest of the session continue with different material
options.misconception: grants what was asked, and so removes the disagreement instead of sustaining something the group can argue about

options.text: She attends and says nothing, which keeps her objection from being imposed on the members who did not share it
options.misconception: makes the objection a private matter, so a group that wanted to hear it has no way of knowing there was one

options.text: She raises the objection after the session, which keeps a distressing passage out of the room without concealing what happened
options.misconception: defers the objection until the discussion it concerned is over, so the group decides on the text before hearing the account

questions.explanation: The criterion is whether the group gets something to do. A member who names the passage and the feature of it she objects to has given the room a claim, and the group can then ask whether the objection is about the text or the situation, whether the same feature would be objectionable elsewhere, and what a group that reads it should do. The other three each resolve the discomfort by a means, and each resolution removes the disagreement from the room while removing it from the record. None of them is base, and members will choose differently. The second is often the right outcome and should be recorded as a decision the group took, rather than arriving as a silence nobody discussed.
questions.hint: Ask which response leaves the group with a claim rather than with a decision already taken.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A member told the group talked past her
questions.learningObjective: classify a charge of unfairness and say what the group must examine
questions.stem: A member is told that the group talked past her for an entire evening. Four readings of the exchange follow. Which one is right?

options.text: The claim is a claim about a pattern in the record, so the pattern is what has to be examined before the charge is accepted or refused
The claim is about the group's intentions, so a group that meant well has already satisfied the norm that applies to how it treats members
options.misconception: makes intention the test, and leaves the record the group could consult unexamined

options.text: The claim is a private report of a feeling, and a group cannot check how a person experienced an evening she was present for
options.misconception: declines to examine anything, and so treats a partly checkable claim as wholly uncheckable

options.text: The claim is a difference of view about the discussion, and it belongs on a later agenda rather than in a reply tonight
options.misconception: reclassifies a charge as an ordinary disagreement, and postpones the question it raises

questions.explanation: The claim is about something the group did, and what a group did is on the record: how many turns the member had, whether her points were answered, who spoke after her. That record will not show how the evening felt, and the exchange should not pretend otherwise, but it will show whether the pattern she describes happened. A group that examines it has a way of responding that does not depend on anyone's state of mind, which is why this is the reading worth acting on. The second option is the standard the group will reach for, and it is the reason unfairness can persist through a term of members meaning well.
questions.hint: Ask whether the group could look up what happened before deciding what to think about it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A report contradicted by the transcript
questions.learningObjective: classify a claim about a term and say what the record requires
questions.stem: A group's report describes a term as inclusive, and its transcript shows two members not spoken after their first turn all term. Four ways of reading this follow. Which one is right?

options.text: The report makes a claim about the whole term and the transcript is the evidence about it, so the two have to be brought into line
The report describes an intention rather than an outcome, and an intention that was not realised is still evidence that the group meant to include
options.misconception: recasts a claim about what happened as a claim about what was intended, and so makes the transcript irrelevant

options.text: The transcript records particular sessions, and a term is judged on all of them together rather than on a selection
options.misconception: argues about the sample, and leaves unexamined that the selection shows two members silenced throughout

options.text: The report was written for readers outside the seminar, and a claim made for outsiders is held to a looser standard
options.misconception: supplies a laxity the report does not claim, and applies it to a document the group itself wrote

questions.explanation: A report that says a term was inclusive is making a claim about what happened, and the group's own transcript is the evidence about what happened. A selection of sessions might or might not be representative, but here the pattern runs through the term, which removes the sampling objection entirely. The group may well conclude that the term was more inclusive than the pattern suggests, and it can then say so in a way that shows it knows about the pattern. The second option is the one worth pressing on, because intention and outcome are genuinely different goods, and a report about an outcome cannot be defended by pointing to the intention behind it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the report is describing something the group did or something the group meant.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Two members disputing a figure
questions.learningObjective: select the appropriate way to settle a disputed factual claim
questions.stem: Two members dispute whether a figure rose or fell across a decade, and neither has the records. Four ways of settling the question follow. Which one is appropriate?

options.text: The records are produced, since a claim about a figure is settled by what the record shows and not by the standing of either disputant
The member who supplied the figure keeps it, since attaching a number to a claim has already met the threshold for making the claim
options.misconception: treats the presence of a number as its own warrant, and makes assertion do the work of evidence

options.text: The question is left open, since a figure that cannot be checked inside the seminar is not one a seminar is expected to settle
options.misconception: infers from the group's present inability to check that the question cannot be checked at all

options.text: The figure the group's own field uses most often is adopted, since a shared convention is the agreed way of reading a number of that kind
options.misconception: substitutes a convention about the wording for a check of the value, and settles nothing

questions.explanation: A disputed figure is a factual dispute, and factual disputes have the useful property that something exists which would end them. Both members would accept the records if the records were produced, which is the test a group can apply immediately by asking whether a record would settle it. Where the answer is yes, not producing the record is a choice, and the group should say so rather than treat the question as beyond it. The fourth option is a real practice and worth distinguishing, because a convention can settle what a term like a category boundary means. It cannot settle whether a number went up.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two disputants would both accept the same document if it turned up.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Responding to a reply that names motives
questions.learningObjective: order the steps for returning a displaced claim to a discussion
questions.stem: A seminar must respond to a reply that names one member's motives instead of answering her claim. Put the steps in the order that lets each depend on the one before it.

options.text: Set the remark aside and name the claim it displaced, since the group cannot return to a question it has not established was left open
Ask the speaker to state her claim, since a claim that has not been restated cannot be the object of a renewed argument
Put that claim back into the discussion on its merits, since a norm about personal remarks sets a remark aside and does not end the exchange
Record both the remark and the claim it displaced, since a norm enforced without a trace is one nobody can check at the end of the term

questions.explanation: The order runs from identifying what was lost to making sure the record shows it. The remark has to be set aside first and named as a remark, because until the group has done that it does not know the exchange has been interrupted rather than continued. It then has to know what claim is now unanswered, which means the speaker restates it rather than the group reconstructing it from memory, since a restatement is also the test of whether the claim still stands. The claim then goes back into the discussion, and only after it has been argued does the record have something worth keeping. Recording first would preserve a gap rather than close it.
questions.hint: Ask which step, done first, would leave the group unable to say what the exchange was about.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Reconciling a report with the group's own record
questions.learningObjective: order the steps for correcting a document the record contradicts
questions.stem: A group's report is contradicted by its own transcript. Put the steps in the order that lets each depend on the one before it.

options.text: Establish what the report claims and what the transcript shows, since the size of the disagreement decides whether this is an error or a difference of emphasis
Establish which parts of the report the transcript leaves standing, since a correction should not discard everything along with the part that is wrong
Decide what the report should say, keeping what stands and removing or qualifying what does not
Publish the corrected version, since a report revised in private and left standing is a report its readers will see uncorrected

questions.explanation: Each step here is a check on the one before it, and the sequence exists to stop a group over-correcting. Establishing the disagreement has to come first because a report and a transcript can conflict in two very different ways: the report may have claimed something the record contradicts, or it may have described the same thing in a stronger way. A group that skips to rewriting will sometimes discard a document that was largely accurate. Establishing what survives comes next, and only then the revision, which is the only step where judgement is genuinely exercised. Publishing last matters as much as any other, since the point of the whole sequence is that the document readers receive is the corrected one.
questions.hint: Ask which step, done last, would leave the defect in front of the report's readers.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Deciding whether to keep a discussion rule
questions.learningObjective: order the steps for reviewing an adopted discussion norm
questions.stem: A group must decide whether to keep a discussion rule it adopted last year. Put the steps in the order that lets each depend on the one before it.

options.text: State what the rule was adopted to secure, since a rule whose purpose cannot be written down cannot be weighed against anything
List what the rule has cost the group, since the alternative is being compared against a record rather than against an expectation
Ask which of those costs the rule offsets, since only the costs it buys are an argument for keeping it
Decide and write down the reason, since a decision with no stated reason cannot be revisited when the membership changes

questions.explanation: The sequence is a comparison and the order protects it. Stating the purpose first is what makes the list of costs legible, since a cost only means something against something the rule was meant to achieve. Collecting the costs next, from the record rather than from memory of how the year felt, keeps the group from deciding on the basis of a single irritating evening. The third step is where the comparison actually happens, and it is easy to skip by treating all costs as equal. The decision and its reason come last together, and the reason is what the next group will have to work with, because a rule that survives a term without a recorded reason is a rule nobody is actually choosing to keep.
questions.hint: Ask which step, done first, would leave the group comparing two things it had not described.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A recording used beyond what was agreed
questions.learningObjective: order the steps for handling a consent problem after the fact
questions.stem: A recording of a seminar session turns up outside the group. Put the steps in the order that lets each depend on the one before it.

options.text: Establish what the group actually agreed about recording, since the scope of that agreement is the question in dispute
Establish what has since been done with the recording, since what has to be undone depends on how far the file has travelled
Ask members what they understood the agreement to cover, since the written record of it and the recollection of it are separate evidence
Agree a rule on reuse before the next session, since a group that only settles the past has nothing governing what happens next time

questions.explanation: The order here is driven by what depends on what. The scope of the original agreement has to come first, because it determines whether the present situation is a breach, a stretch, or a plain misunderstanding about what was asked. What has happened to the file comes next, because the remedy differs sharply depending on whether it was viewed once by the group or is circulating beyond anyone who agreed to anything. The members' recollections follow, and they matter precisely because the written record of a question put in a room and met with silence is thin. The forward rule comes last on purpose: a group that spends the whole meeting on the past will arrive at the next recording with the same ambiguity.
questions.hint: Ask which step, done first, would leave the group fixing something before knowing what is broken.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: How a fair rule can cost some members
questions.learningObjective: explain why a rule that improves fairness overall can still leave members worse off
questions.stem: Explain why a discussion rule can make a seminar fairer overall and still leave particular members worse off than they were before it.

answer.exemplar: A rule that redistributes floor time, turns, or the right to be heard cannot help everyone at once, because the help is comparative. Two minutes a turn is a great deal of time to a member who arrived with the chapter annotated and very little to a member who is still working out what the question is, and the rule treats those two members as though the two minutes were the same resource. The first thing to say, then, is that such a rule is neutral between positions rather than between people, and neutrality of that kind leaves standing where it was. Members who notice this are not complaining about the chair, because the chair is applying the rule exactly as written; they are noticing that a rule which sounded as though it treated everyone alike in fact took from one kind of participant in order to give to another. The second thing to say concerns what the rule was written against. A rule aimed at the confident member who takes every turn will also shorten the turns of members who were merely persistent, and nothing in the rule distinguishes the two, since persistence and domination look the same from the chair's chair. Neither of these observations makes such rules wrong. It makes them trades, and the practical consequence is that a group adopting one should say aloud what it is trading and for what, so that the members paying the price know the price was chosen rather than overlooked, and so that next year's group can reverse the decision on the evidence rather than on the memory of a bad evening.

questions.explanation: A strong response identifies that a rule about airtime or turns distributes rather than enlarges, notes that neutrality between positions is not neutrality between people, and connects the cost to what the rule was written against, since a rule aimed at domination also catches persistence. It should add that none of this makes the rule wrong, only that it is a trade, and that the fix is to state the trade openly so it can be reviewed later on evidence.
questions.hint: Ask what a rule gives to one member by taking from another, and what it was aimed at when it was written.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: How a well-run group can end with nothing argued
questions.learningObjective: explain how a group can follow every norm and still fail to test a claim
questions.stem: Explain how a group can observe every discussion norm it has written and still finish an evening without having tested a single claim.

answer.exemplar: The reason is that most discussion norms govern moves inside an argument rather than the occurrence of arguments, and nothing among them requires an argument to happen. A group can interrupt nobody, disparage nobody, cite every opponent generously, and treat every self-description with respect, and still spend ninety minutes on a sequence of positions each stated once and never met. Each norm has been obeyed, because none of them was about whether a claim got an answer. What is missing is a norm about the exchange rather than about the speakers, and it takes a particular form: that a claim made in the room is answered before the group moves on, that an objection carries something to argue with, and that a member who holds the counter-case is given the floor to put it. Groups usually discover this the hard way, at the end of a term in which everyone has been scrupulous and nothing has been settled, and the discovery is nearly always made by the member who asks a question and finds that nobody is disagreeing with anything. It is worth adding why the gap is easy to miss. Compliance with a written norm feels like the work of a discussion, and it produces a session that goes smoothly, ends on time, and leaves everyone able to recall that nobody was rude. The repair is unglamorous and small, and it is also the only version that works: require each claim to be met before the floor moves, and keep a record of which claims were met so that the term's minutes show the difference between a busy room and an argued one.

questions.explanation: A strong response identifies that norms about treatment constrain conduct inside an argument without requiring an argument, and contrasts that with a norm about the exchange itself, such as requiring every claim to be answered before the room moves on. It should explain why the gap is easy to miss, since compliance feels like discussion and produces a smooth session, and should finish with the procedural repair and a way of recording whether claims were actually met.
questions.hint: Ask whether any of the group's norms is about what happens to a claim, rather than about how members treat one another.
